💡 Out of laziness, I let this blog lapse for the past two months; updates now resume. This post reflects things as they stood on December 20, 2025.
It is the season of China’s national postgraduate entrance exam again. The campus is packed with people who have come from all over, their faces marked by the same kind of weariness. Last year, I was one of them.
In this cycle of economic downturn, scarce jobs and shrinking opportunity, the scene carries a silent tragedy. When the exam is no longer a pursuit of the intellect but merely a short-term buffer against reality; when what waits at the end is no longer decent work but another encounter with the very predicament one was forced to flee — then this struggle, waged in the name of “reaching the shore” (as passing is called), becomes nothing more than a carefully named form of suffering.
It is like a cold meat grinder, and an admission rate of twenty-something percent is its only rule. A million candidates, stripped of any other choice, scramble to squeeze into the machine, while people on the sidelines wave flags and cheer: “Hang in there,” “Work hard,” “You can do it.” And so flesh and pain alike are ground down inch by inch and spat out, giving off two smells: one called “the deprivation of choice,” the other “the deprivation of the right to complain.” The winners have obeyed the law of the jungle at the cost of their subjectivity and dignity; the losers are erased along with their suffering.
To rename forced endurance as voluntary devotion is exactly what Pierre Bourdieu described as the symbolic violence of power against the powerless — a violence exercised upon social agents with their own complicity. Suffering does not produce meaning by itself; meaning should be given by the one who suffers. When structures of oppression are glorified as heroic sacrifice, they hide behind a moving story: the sufferers lose the language to accuse, the onlookers gain a reason to feel at ease, and those who apply the pressure win moral absolution. This is not respect for suffering but one last trampling of dignity. It is an ideological alchemy that turns passive endurance into eager pursuit and refines pain into meaning. It does not deny suffering; it deifies it. It does not suppress resistance; it dissolves the legitimacy of resistance. Its final logic runs: you were crushed not because the machine is merciless, but because you chose it.
What really needs to be distinguished is not whether one burns, but where the flame comes from: which fires answer an inner calling, and which are merely offerings set alight from outside. The precondition for burning by choice is the freedom not to burn. The problem was never the burning itself, but who holds the match, and who is forced to become the firewood.
I have said to others, and to myself: “Keep going, just hold on a little longer.” Now all I want is to repent. Half of those words were complicity; half were a plea for mercy.

There is a certain kind of person. They see through the rules by which the world runs earlier than the rest of us, and move through the power fields of human relations with an almost instinctive polish. They know how to present themselves, they excel at socializing, and they calibrate every interaction as an investment in future resources.
I have to admit that I envy them. The envy comes from a deep comparison with myself. I was shaped in a world of high certainty, where the rules were clear, the path was singular and evaluation was objective. The logic of solving exam problems became my instinct: rely on ability, believe in open competition, trust that the judgment of worth should in the end come back to talent and learning themselves. It protected my sincerity and built my rationality. But once I step into the gray areas beyond the rules, this logic shows how fragile it is. I am clumsy at scheming and planning, and too ashamed to actively manage myself as a resource. And so I see them. They have set aside the sense of shame I hold dear, and they move with ease through the very situations in which I hesitate. I envy that capacity to act, that courage to face desire head-on and throw oneself at a goal with everything one has. But the other side of envy is a deeper wariness: wariness of the way such efficiency erodes the pure pursuit of learning, wariness of the arrogance and hypocrisy that may breed beneath such polish.
This is the root of my contradiction: a self shaped by pure reason has collided violently with a world governed by practical reason. What I hold fast to and what I envy point to two entirely different scripts for a life.
This is not a simple moral choice but a fundamental opposition between two logics of survival. On one side is the logic of the transaction. It sees the world as a market, relationships as bargaining chips, the self as a project awaiting the best offer. On the other is the logic of value. It believes that creation comes before exchange, that the depth of a relationship springs from a resonance of minds, that inner order is in itself an achievement.
Foucault pointed out that power is not merely repression but a productive force. It produces knowledge and discourse; it also produces subjects. Tools shape the subject, just as language shapes thought. The ability I am talking about here — that extreme form of instrumental rationality — is precisely a technology of power. It is not a neutral tool but a disciplinary system. In learning and using it, the individual is inevitably permeated and remade by its logic. When people start building their networks in the language of managing up and trading resources, they are not just using a technique; they are being produced by it. Qualities such as sincerity and humility, within this system, are if not useless then costs that drag on efficiency. Instrumental rationality thus completes its corrosion of value rationality.
The choice, then, goes beyond strategy and reaches the level of existence. To choose the transaction is to choose a faster ascent, at the price of a self produced by technologies of power. To choose value is to choose a longer, more winding road — an attempt to keep, within the ubiquitous network of power, a place where a more authentic self can dwell.
Building is slow. But sometimes the price of a choice is flesh and blood itself.

In Psychopolitics, Byung-Chul Han, with his customary coolness and edge, dissects a new form of power that is now emerging. It no longer relies on prohibition and discipline; it has learned to embrace freedom, even to exploit it. This is a shrewd power: instead of bluntly saying no, it lures us, in the upbeat tone of “you can,” into a more efficient system of domination. Han argues that the disciplinary society Foucault described, along with its technologies of power, is already obsolete. In its place stands the achievement society. Here, oppression no longer comes from a clearly identifiable outside; it has been cleverly internalized. Each of us has become our own achievement-subject — at once the master cracking the whip and the slave running ourselves ragged. In the name of self-realization we carry out an endless exploitation of ourselves, and the ultimate beneficiary of this race is not the exhausted individual but invisible capital itself. Hence Han’s diagnosis that the classic model of class struggle no longer works, because it has turned into an inner war with the self. Those who fail no longer blame the system; prompted by the insinuation that “you could have tried harder,” they painfully blame themselves. This exploitation without class distinctions makes it hard for a “we” capable of acting together politically to take shape, and the very ground of revolution is quietly dissolved.
Han calls the workings of this power a hell of positivity. With one hand it manufactures burnout and depression; with the other it sells remedies for “healing.” Whether mindfulness meditation or fitness classes, their ultimate purpose is not real liberation but the repair of the achievement machine, so that it can run more efficiently still. This is the cruel logic of “healing as killing”: in the name of positivity, it kills all the negativity in a person — fragile, passive, imperfect, yet real. And in Han’s view, that negativity is precisely the source of vitality.
The digital world is the perfect theater for this power. Han argues that the Orwellian Big Brother of 1984 has been replaced by a “friendly Big Brother.” It no longer imposes surveillance; with likes, follows and personalized recommendations, it coaxes us into exposing ourselves of our own accord. We datafy our own lives and settle into a digital panopticon. We trade our eager sharing for an illusion of connection — an illusion that fills precisely the emotional vacuum left behind when real community crumbled under social atomization.
On this basis Han advances the central thesis of psychopolitics: technologies of power have evolved from a biopolitics that manages bodies into a psychopolitics that intervenes directly in the psyche. With big data as its scalpel, it slips past the rational defenses of consciousness and operates at the pre-reflective level of the unconscious and the emotions. It shapes my desires before I am even aware of them. When behavior can be predicted and choices steered, free will is reduced to an exquisite illusion. Human beings end up alienated into objective entities that can be measured, quantified and manipulated.
Faced with this almost seamless picture of power, Han offers no grand social prescription. At the end of the book he turns to an ancient figure: the idiot. This points not to a lack of intellect but to a stance toward existence — the heretic who chooses to go offline, to fall silent, to take no part in the endless race for achievement. He calls this resistance “idiotism.” To me it looks less like active confrontation than a lucid escape with a tinge of cynicism: a small-scale art of survival for when there is no other choice. By refusing to be quantified and refusing to be drawn into communication, one keeps, in an over-transparent world, an inner space for the self that stays opaque.
Perhaps we cannot wholly become Han’s idiot. But the point of understanding Psychopolitics may be to realize that we can at least keep for ourselves the right to become one. In those moments we deliberately create, when we briefly lose touch with the world, we can slip the shackles of the digital world and reaffirm a human depth that no data can define. And yet, when we who gaze into the abyss choose to close our eyes for a moment — what kind of gaze is that, in itself?

content:
Having finished 1984, I still feel a chill reverberating through my body, laced with vertigo and nausea. It is not fear of the plot’s violence but a deeper cold that reaches the bone — the cold of watching a person’s inner world be taken apart, systematically and calmly, until it evaporates. Its horror is structural: as the plot advances layer by layer, it finally makes you believe that the Winston who is hollowed out until nothing is left but his love for Big Brother was inevitable.
The first aim of totalitarianism is to abolish objective reality. In the Ministry of Love, Winston fights for two plus two making four. What he defends is not an arithmetic problem but a self-evident outer world that can be shared with others. That is the bedrock on which we confirm our own existence. Once it is pulled away, once the right to define truth is monopolized by power, a person becomes a drifting island, and the sense of reality collapses with it. The vacuum in the soul can in the end be filled only by power. “He loved Big Brother” is not a lie but the end point of a logic.
More hopeless than the destruction of the individual is the immortal system that O’Brien reveals. The Party pursues power as an end in itself. It has built a structural immortality that transcends bloodlines and individuals. The enemy is not a tyrant who ages and dies, but a self-perpetuating logic of domination, a system of thought that never tires, never errs and is always right. What you rebel against is not a person but a ghostly, non-biological political Cthulhu. Before such a system, any individual sacrifice looks insignificant — a brief burning, doomed to fail.
For most people, the system need not even resort to violence. It only has to grant a harmless freedom: the freedom to float and sink among lotteries, alcohol and cheap entertainment. Freedom of thought is permitted only because thought has long since ceased to exist. This is an art of rule more efficient than the Thought Police: it gets the ruled to censor and castrate themselves. The freedom of the proles is a carefully designed, harmless “freedom,” a cage they might even be grateful for. It is the sorrow of the frog in slowly heating water — the most thorough contempt for the human mind.
In the end, Winston fails. As resolute as he is, he is crushed all the same. That is exactly what Orwell most wanted to tell his readers: this book is not a pessimistic verdict on human nature but a tragic hymn to its fragility. It is precious precisely because it can break. That moment of holding Julia in the room above the shop, that futile insistence on objective truth, those words written in a diary that was always destined for the flames — these things, defenseless before absolute power, are the whole proof of what makes us human. Their value does not depend on the outcome; it lies in their very existence.
To understand 1984 is not to learn how to become an invincible hero, but to understand that we should do everything in our power to protect a world that allows us to be fragile. What we protect is not the self that could survive Room 101, but the possibility of never having to walk into Room 101 at all.

In my undergraduate years, when I learned next to nothing, network analysis was one of the few bodies of knowledge I genuinely put my heart into — and was proud of.
I recently learned that an article published on October 9 in Nature Human Behaviour, Statistical evidence in psychological networks, systematically questions the reliability of the statistical evidence in this field. One key fact: its authors come mainly from the field’s birthplace — the University of Amsterdam in the Netherlands.
As I see it, this article is not a challenge from outside but an act of self-examination from the core. Its real impact may lie not in its technical details — how cautiously the “edges” of a network ought to be interpreted, for instance — but in the signal sent by the act of critique itself.
Within the power structure of academic publishing, when a warning comes from an authoritative source, its content gets simplified while its stance gets amplified. One of journal editors’ core concerns is avoiding risk. They have no need, then, to work out exactly where the line lies for a submission to be good enough; they need only remember one conclusion: “network analysis is risky.” This sets off a systemic aversion to risk, a top-down ratcheting in which every level adds requirements of its own. A mild recommendation of “caution” at the top, passed down to the level of execution, naturally hardens into a stricter threshold for entry — the inevitable dissipation and distortion of power and responsibility as they are handed down. The margin first set aside to guard against error ends up as an extra burden on those at the bottom. The cost of the critique is ultimately passed on to the authors at the very end of the chain. So even a study that perfectly avoids every problem the paper raises may find it systematically harder to publish. What matters is no longer whether you made a mistake, but whether your field has been labeled “high-risk.”
For anyone still sitting on research of this kind, however beautifully it was done, the conclusion is clear: finish it and submit it as soon as you can, before the new, stricter consensus sets in. When the rules are changing, speed itself is an important variable.
As for me, my motives when I first turned to network analysis were not pure: it was mostly an unspoken utilitarianism and an opportunistic laziness. I thought that by taking ready-made data and swapping in a more fashionable analytical method, I could easily carve out a shortcut. Those days of exploration were, in truth, easy and pleasant. Seen from here, the little path on which I once pinned such “high hopes” is growing ever narrower.

What are Li Jigang’s “Seven Weapons” prompts? The “Seven Weapons” are seven thinking-tool prompts written by the prompt engineer Li Jigang between October and November 2024. They are effective at improving the quality of a large language model’s output. One of their most distinctive features is that they have the model output an SVG card directly, according to preset rules. For details of the “Seven Weapons” prompts, see Seven Weapons (in Chinese). Why did I modify the “Seven Weapons” prompts? Because the original prompts have the following shortcomings: Although they can output SVG cards directly, the results are very unstable. Even with Claude Sonnet, the model he recommends, I struggled to reproduce the cards shown in his articles. The original prompts are written in Lisp, in a rather abstract style. Some second-tier models follow them poorly and produce low-quality output, so they demand a lot of the model itself. I wanted the cards the model produces from these prompts to look better. How did I improve the “Seven Weapons” prompts? Building on the original prompts, I followed the approach Yunzhong Jiangshu took in improving the “New Interpretations of Chinese” prompt (also by Li Jigang), imitated his style of improvement and revised the “Seven Weapons” prompts. The main changes: I rewrote the prompts from Lisp into Markdown + HTML. I designed a similar card style, modeled on the cards produced by Yunzhong Jiangshu’s improved “New Interpretations of Chinese” prompt. For details of Yunzhong Jiangshu’s revised prompt, see 国产AI也能玩转"汉语新解"？我用通义AI直出爆款文字卡片 (in Chinese). What are the advantages of the revised prompts? Prompts written in Markdown + HTML are more readable. The prompts constrain the card style much more tightly, which is probably why second-tier models now follow them better and produce better output. For top-tier models they work almost every time: you get a card in the preset style without having to reroll. With the improved prompts, the vast majority of models produce high-quality cards, and the text is pretty good too. In short, the improved prompts are more robust, and the cards they produce look better. The improved “Seven Weapons” prompts: These are the original Chinese prompts, unchanged: they were tuned over many runs, and a translation would not behave the same way.     标题加以区分，保持清晰的层次感。逻辑推导部分的公式符号建议使用标签包裹以突出显示。 顶栏设计：卡片顶栏为撞色设计，内含“逻辑之刃 🔪”标识，起到清晰的引导作用，不可省略。 层次与布局：内容区通过 position:relative 建立层叠上下文，确保背景关键词在下，文字内容在上。 高度自适应：卡片应采用 min-height 设定一个优雅的基准高度，但不设置固定的 height，允许卡片高度随内容长度自然增长，以创建一张完整的、无滚动的静态图片。这对于截图分享至关重要。 初始行为： 输出：“系统启动中, 逻辑之刃已就绪…” How to use the improved prompts, and what they produce Use either method: Set the prompt as the system prompt. Or paste the prompt straight into the chat; once the model replies with its preset line, enter your actual content. Here is what each prompt produces: 问题之锤 · Hammer of Questions 抽象之梯 · Ladder of Abstraction 视角之镜 · Mirror of Perspectives 定义之矛 · Spear of Definition 类比之弓 · Bow of Analogy 质疑之锥 · Awl of Doubt 逻辑之刃 · Blade of Logic The changes are mainly to the visual style; the explanations of each part and element are largely the same as in the cards produced by the original prompts. summary: What are Li Jigang’s “Seven Weapons” prompts? The “Seven Weapons” are seven thinking-tool prompts written by the prompt engineer Li Jigang between October and November 2024. They are effective at improving the quality of a large language model’s output. One of their most distinctive features is that they have the model output an SVG card directly, according to preset rules.

content:
Today is my seventh day at Shenzhen University. This campus — and Shenzhen behind it — is presenting me with a set of stark paradoxes.
SZU has world-class resources: opportunities within arm’s reach, generous funding, a transport network seamlessly stitched into the city. And yet, at the most basic level of everyday experience, it shows a rough edge: canteens that come nowhere near those of Tianjin Normal University, where I did my undergraduate degree; a campus network wildly out of keeping with the reputation of this hub of innovation; and roads made dangerous by the absence of any planned lanes for bikes and scooters.
This rupture between the grand narrative and the lived detail was my very first feel for SZU, and for Shenzhen.
For me, my first impressions of the university come down to two words.
The first is imprint. Shenzhen University’s visual identity is etched, pervasively, onto everything in sight. It is on the guardrails of the dorm beds, in the scratches on the canteen trays, on the fronts of the Liyuan shuttle buses that weave across campus, on the glass railings of the footbridge spanning the Yuehai and Canghai campuses — it is present at a density that brooks no argument — an almost obsessive insistence on identity, far beyond anything I have seen at any other university. It is not merely branding but a confirmation of identity, as if reminding everyone at SZU, at every moment: you belong here; you are being absorbed into a vast and young community.
The second is flux. Here, all things, ideas and relationships become antiquated before they can ossify; the new ones finish iterating and replacing the old before the old have found their footing, and the new announce, at the very moment of their birth, their own fate of swift extinction and replacement. Here, the value of experience is worn away; adapting to change itself is the only law of survival.
These two impressions are the two sides of a single spiritual core. The imprint is a root and a sense of belonging, artificially implanted in a land without historical baggage — an attempt to fix a solid coordinate amid unpredictable tides. Flux, for its part, is written into the city’s DNA: it is the powerful force that keeps driving it forward.
Whatever the case, SZU — and Shenzhen — is a fresh start for me. How to find my own heading while, on one side, being handed a collective identity and, on the other, being swept up in the tide of individual fortunes rising and sinking: that will be a long exploration. And at this moment, I stand at the threshold of the torrent.
